newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Asia beef import market forecast to grow-AMLC.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Asia beef import market forecast to grow-AMLC.

text.p: Asian beef demand in 1997 is forecast to continue to rise, opening opportunities for Australia as the largest world exporter, the Australian Meat and Livestock Corp (AMLC) said in its Meat and Livestock Review.
Preliminary figures for 1996 showed that Australia increased its world beef export market share by 2.8 percentage points to 22.7 percent in 1996, the AMLC said.
This was up from a 19.9 percent share ten years ago.

However, Australia's position as the dominant trader was being challenged by significant inroads made by the United States, which increased its market share to a preliminary 18.5 percent in 1996 from 5.9 percent in 1986, the AMLC said.
The U.S. is forecast to continue to exploit market opportunities through 1997, it said.

Major players in world beef export trade in 1996 were Australia with 1.1 million tonnes of exports, the U.S. with 894,000 tonnes, the European Union with 578,000 tonnes, New Zealand with 505,000 tonnes and Argentina with 450,000 tonnes, it said.

While Australia has been the largest volume exporter of beef for the past ten years, with shipments averaging 1.2 million tonnes a year, the rate of growth in beef shipments seemed to have stagnated, the AMLC said.
Australia's 1996 production of beef and veal, at about 1.8 million tonnes, was 11 percent above 1986, while consumption at 680,000 tonnes was 2.3 percent ahead of ten years ago.
U.S. beef production since 1994 had been on a steady rise, reaching an estimated 11.8 million tonnes in 1996, it said.
"The result has been a growing proportion of high quality beef offered by the U.S. on the world market, at very competitive prices," the AMLC said.

Argentina's 1997 beef exports are expected to rise to 480,000 tonnes in 1997 from 450,000 tonnes in 1996, it said. This would result from the granting by the U.S. of a 20,000 tonne import quota, allowing the first Argentinian beef exports to the U.S. in more than 60 years. Other countries were expected to follow the U.S. move tio allow imports of Argentine beef, the AMLC said.
"It is hoped that beef demand will recover, at least partially, during 1997," AMLC said.
"There are also signs of some liquidation of the U.S. herd thus reducing the competitive pressure.
"Competition for ... expanding international markets will remain intense (for) Australia. Evidently, 1997 is poised to offer ongoing challenges for the Australian beef industry," the AMLC said.
